contextual-advertising.mainHtml:
CONTEXTUAL ADVERTISING

Contextual Advertising That Understands the Environment Before the Impression

Align ads with the meaning, subject and suitability of content using contextual signals and AI-assisted semantic analysis — without making behavioral identity the only route to relevance.

Plan a Contextual CampaignSee AI Programmatic
What is contextual advertising?

Contextual advertising places or prioritizes ads based on the content environment and related signals, such as topic, semantics, page type or suitability, rather than depending only on a user’s past behavior.

CONTEXT LAYERS

From page meaning to media decision

1

Topic

Identify the broad subject area of the page, content or media environment.

2

Semantics

Look beyond keywords to understand meaning, relationships and likely context.

3

Suitability

Apply brand, category and campaign rules to decide where an ad should or should not appear.

4

Creative fit

Choose messaging and format that make sense for the environment and screen.

CONTEXTUAL ≠ BEHAVIORAL

Relevance can come from the environment itself.

Behavioral targeting can use historical user signals. Contextual targeting focuses on the content and environment around the ad opportunity. A campaign may use one approach, the other, or a permitted combination depending on strategy and applicable requirements.

WHERE AI HELPS

AI can improve semantic interpretation, not create certainty.

Machine learning can help classify and compare content at scale, but suitability rules, quality review and campaign context still matter.

Practical guardrailA contextual model should support campaign decisions, not be presented as perfectly understanding every page or guaranteeing brand safety.
USE CASES

Where contextual planning becomes useful

Content-aligned campaigns

Reach environments that closely match the product, service or message theme.

Brand-suitability controls

Apply inclusion and exclusion logic around categories or content environments.

Cross-screen relevance

Carry contextual planning into display, video, CTV or other eligible media environments.

BANGLADESH + INTERNATIONAL

Context is local, even when the campaign is global.

Language, culture, publisher environments and media patterns can vary significantly across Bangladesh and international markets. Contextual models and campaign rules should reflect the market being activated.

Semantic relevance should be market-aware

Explore how contextual signals can be prioritized

Use a simple educational model to compare topical relevance, brand suitability, recency and page-quality inputs for a contextual placement.

This score is not an auction score, ranking signal or production model. It demonstrates how multiple contextual inputs can be combined conceptually.

RICH MEDIA ADVERTISING

Rich Media Advertising for Interactive, High-Impact Creative Experiences

Go beyond static display with HTML5-powered interactions, multi-panel stories, carousel experiences, cube/3D motion, parallax, video-enabled formats and other high-impact creative — matched to eligible placements and screens.

Launch Rich MediaBrowse HTML5 Formats
Rich media is a creative system, not one ad size
  • Interactive states and motion
  • Multi-frame or multi-panel storytelling
  • Video and high-impact executions
  • Placement-specific technical validation
FORMAT FAMILIES

Build the experience around how people can actually interact

Carousel & multi-panel

Sequence multiple messages, products or creative states inside one interactive experience.

Cube / 3D

Use dimensional transitions to reveal multiple faces, messages or product views where supported.

Parallax & motion

Create depth and movement that responds to scroll or placement behavior, subject to device and publisher requirements.

Expandable & high-impact

Use larger or changing creative states only where the placement, inventory policy and user experience allow it.

Video-enabled HTML5

Custom interactive concepts

From idea to validated runtime

01

Rich media works best when the format earns attention through useful interaction and strong storytelling, not by obstructing content or forcing unnecessary motion.

HTML5 AD FORMATS

HTML5 Ad Formats for Responsive, Interactive Programmatic Creative

Build display creative with motion, interaction and responsive behavior using HTML5 — from standard animated units to carousel, cube/3D, parallax, expandable, multi-state and video-enabled executions.

HTML5 format guide

HTML5 describes the creative runtime technology. The actual ad format also depends on dimensions, interaction model, asset weight, click behavior, publisher rules and the inventory where the creative will run.

FORMAT TAXONOMY

From standard motion to advanced interaction

Animated display

Lightweight motion and transitions inside standard display dimensions.

Carousel / multi-frame

Multiple panels or frames for products, features or sequential storytelling.

Cube / 3D

Dimensional transitions that reveal multiple creative faces or states.

Parallax

Layered motion that creates depth in response to scroll or placement behavior.

Expandable

A creative state that can open into a larger canvas where the publisher and device permit it.

Video-enabled

HTML5 units that incorporate video playback or video-led interaction in eligible placements.

TECHNICAL READINESS

A good format still needs a clean build

CheckWhy it mattersWhat to validate
Dimensions
Inventory accepts defined creative sizes
Canvas size, responsive behavior, safe areas
Asset weight
Heavy creative can hurt load and user experience
Image/video compression, initial load, lazy assets
Click behavior
Interaction and navigation must be intentional
Clickthrough URL, interaction zones, accidental taps
Runtime behavior
Motion and scripts must remain stable
Animation loops, fallback state, device support

01

Format choice

Select the interaction pattern that supports the campaign idea.

02

Asset mapping

Prepare copy, images, logos, video and state-specific elements.

Creative QA

Run only where the technical and publisher requirements are compatible.

AI & Programmatic

The Future of Programmatic Advertising: AI-Driven Campaigns

How AI is changing programmatic advertising through bidding, contextual intelligence, forecasting, creative decisioning and accountable optimization.

Boost RAVA publishes educational content for advertisers and publishers. Examples explain strategy and technology; they are not performance guarantees.

AI is becoming an operating layer for programmatic advertising

Programmatic advertising already automates auctions, targeting and delivery, but artificial intelligence changes how decisions are made inside that automation. Instead of relying only on fixed rules, AI systems can evaluate patterns across contextual signals, campaign events, placement quality, time, device and conversion behaviour. The practical value is not that a machine replaces media strategy. The value is that a campaign can process more signals, test more combinations and react faster than a manually managed workflow.

For advertisers in Bangladesh and international markets, this matters because media conditions are rarely static. Inventory changes by hour, audience behaviour changes by device, and a creative that works in one environment may underperform in another. An AI-assisted programmatic workflow can continuously compare those conditions against the campaign objective while keeping human controls around budget, brand suitability and measurement.

Where AI contributes across the campaign workflow

AI can support several layers of a programmatic campaign: bid estimation, pacing, contextual classification, anomaly detection, creative selection, frequency management and forecast modelling. These capabilities should be treated as decision support rather than proof of guaranteed performance. A model can identify correlations in data, but campaign teams still need to validate whether those patterns make commercial and brand sense.

Contextual intelligence is especially important as advertisers look for ways to improve relevance without depending on unnecessary personal data. A system can interpret the subject and meaning of content, classify an environment and decide whether it matches the campaign brief. That does not eliminate the need for brand-safety controls, but it gives the buying system a richer view of where an ad is appearing.

How AI-optimized programmatic campaigns work

A reliable AI-optimized campaign starts with a clear objective and trustworthy measurement. The buying system needs signals that reflect the actual business goal, whether that is qualified traffic, completed views, leads or another event. Weak or inconsistent signals can teach an optimization model the wrong lesson. Clean event definitions, sensible attribution windows and enough learning time are therefore more important than turning on every available automation feature.

The model then evaluates opportunities against the goal and constraints. During an auction it may estimate the value of an impression, adjust a bid, consider contextual relevance, check delivery pace and choose among eligible creatives. After delivery, new observations feed back into future decisions. The loop is continuous, but responsible campaign management still includes limits, review points and the ability to override the model.

Machine learning does not remove campaign risk

AI can optimize toward the wrong proxy if the measurement design is poor. It can over-concentrate spend when a narrow pocket of inventory appears efficient. It can also reproduce bias present in training data or historical campaign behaviour. Other risks include opaque decisioning, invalid traffic, creative fatigue and excessive frequency. These are reasons to add governance, not reasons to avoid automation entirely.

Campaign teams should document objectives, monitor delivery concentration, review placement quality, compare model-led results against baselines and investigate sudden changes. Brand suitability controls should remain independent from pure performance optimization. Where an automated decision has material commercial impact, the team should be able to explain which signals and rules influenced that decision at an operational level.

AI, rich media, CTV and DOOH are converging

Programmatic buying is no longer limited to standard display placements. HTML5 rich media, online video, connected TV and digital out-of-home can all participate in broader automated media strategies. AI can help coordinate those environments by identifying when and where a campaign should prioritize a format, but creative experience still has to fit the screen.

A carousel, parallax unit or interactive HTML5 execution can offer a different experience from a CTV video or a DOOH screen. Cross-screen optimization should therefore respect creative context rather than treating every impression as interchangeable. The strongest systems connect buying intelligence with format-aware creative delivery.

What advertisers should ask before using AI programmatic technology

Ask what the optimization objective actually is, what data the system uses, how contextual or audience signals are evaluated, how brand-safety controls are applied and how a human can review or override a decision. Ask whether the platform can separate exploration from established performance patterns and how it handles sparse data when a campaign is new.

Advertisers should also understand reporting boundaries. AI-generated predictions and optimization scores are not the same as audited business outcomes. A trustworthy platform should make that distinction clear and avoid presenting illustrative dashboard metrics as guaranteed campaign performance.

Bangladesh and global opportunity

Bangladesh offers a growing digital audience and a media market where local context, language, device mix and price sensitivity can materially affect campaign performance. International advertisers entering the market need local relevance, while Bangladeshi advertisers expanding overseas need cross-market controls. AI can help manage complexity, but it should be combined with market knowledge and transparent measurement.

Boost RAVA positions AI programmatic, contextual advertising, HTML5 rich media, CTV and DOOH as connected capabilities. The goal is to give advertisers and publishers a clearer path from campaign objective to media activation while keeping claims grounded in what the platform can actually support.

Frequently asked questions

Does programmatic advertising use AI? Yes. Many modern programmatic systems use machine learning or other AI techniques for bidding, forecasting, contextual classification, pacing and optimization. The exact capabilities vary by platform.

Is AI programmatic advertising fully autonomous? It can automate many decisions, but responsible campaigns still need human objectives, constraints, brand-safety rules, measurement design and review.

What is the difference between AI programmatic and contextual advertising? AI programmatic is the broader use of AI across automated media buying and optimization. Contextual advertising focuses on matching ads to the meaning and environment of content; AI can be one of the technologies used to understand that context.

What are the main risks? Poor measurement, over-optimization, opaque decisions, biased data, frequency problems and weak placement controls are common risks. Governance and transparent reporting help reduce them.

Publisher Monetization

Header Bidding for Publishers: A Practical Revenue Optimization Guide

A practical guide to header bidding, auction design, demand competition, latency, floor strategy and publisher monetization.

Boost RAVA publishes educational content for advertisers and publishers. Examples explain strategy and technology; they are not performance guarantees.

What header bidding changes for publishers

Header bidding gives multiple demand sources an opportunity to compete before the ad server makes its final decision. The core idea is straightforward: increase transparent competition for an impression instead of relying on a strictly sequential waterfall. For publishers, the opportunity is not simply more bidders. The real value comes from understanding demand quality, auction pressure, latency and how each partner contributes to sustainable revenue.

A healthy setup should be measured across more than headline CPM. Publishers should examine net revenue, fill, timeout behaviour, bid density, viewability, advertiser quality and user experience. A bidder that occasionally produces a high bid but adds significant latency may be less valuable than a consistent partner with strong coverage and clean demand.

How the auction flow works

When a page or app has an eligible impression, the header-bidding layer requests bids from configured demand partners. Those bids arrive within a controlled timeout and are passed into the ad decisioning process. The ad server can then compare eligible demand on a more level basis. The exact architecture varies by client-side, server-side or hybrid implementation, but the publisher still needs clear rules for timeouts, price granularity and bidder participation.

The auction should also respect consent signals, privacy requirements, blocked categories, creative policies and inventory-specific rules. Competition is useful only when it operates inside a controlled marketplace.

Revenue optimization without chasing vanity metrics

Publishers often focus on CPM because it is easy to compare. But higher CPM can coexist with lower total revenue if fill drops or latency damages page engagement. A better approach is to evaluate revenue per thousand sessions, revenue per pageview, bid rate, win rate and the contribution of each demand source after fees and technical costs.

Floor pricing should be tested carefully. Aggressive floors can lift the average winning CPM while reducing auction participation and overall fill. Dynamic or segment-specific floors can be useful, but they should respond to real demand patterns rather than arbitrary targets.

Latency and user experience

Every bidder adds network and processing work. On mobile networks, especially in markets with varied connection quality, poorly managed header bidding can delay ad rendering and affect the page experience. Publishers should enforce realistic timeouts, remove consistently slow partners and monitor the relationship between monetization and Core Web Vitals.

Server-side bidding can reduce browser work, but it also changes cookie matching and observability. There is no universally superior architecture; the right choice depends on traffic, devices, privacy requirements and the publisher's technical stack.

Demand quality, transparency and controls

More demand is not automatically better demand. Publishers need controls for blocked advertisers, malware, misleading creatives, sensitive categories and policy compliance. Sellers.json, supply-chain transparency and clear partner agreements help buyers understand where inventory originates and help publishers maintain a cleaner marketplace.

Reporting should distinguish gross auction value from actual publisher revenue and make discrepancies visible. When multiple systems report the same impression differently, publishers need a reconciliation process rather than assuming one dashboard is authoritative.

Header bidding in Bangladesh and international markets

Publishers in Bangladesh can use header bidding to expose inventory to broader demand while preserving local commercial relationships. Device mix, connection quality, ad sizes, language and local advertiser demand can influence the best configuration. A setup designed for a high-bandwidth desktop-heavy market may not be appropriate for a mobile-heavy audience.

International publishers face similar trade-offs at a larger scale. Regional bidder performance, consent frameworks, currency, time zones and demand seasonality all affect auction outcomes. Segmenting analysis by market is more useful than judging every impression against one global average.

A practical publisher checklist

Start with a limited number of high-quality demand partners, define timeouts, document floor logic, measure latency and reconcile revenue. Review bidder contribution by market and device. Remove partners that add complexity without meaningful incremental value. Keep consent and policy controls close to the auction layer.

Finally, treat header bidding as an ongoing marketplace design problem. Demand changes, browsers change and advertiser requirements change. The strongest publisher teams revisit configuration regularly instead of assuming the initial setup will remain optimal forever.

Frequently asked questions

Does header bidding always increase revenue? No. It can increase competition, but results depend on demand quality, implementation, latency and inventory. No uplift should be assumed or guaranteed.

Is server-side header bidding faster? It can reduce browser-side work, but the full outcome depends on infrastructure, partner matching and network conditions.

How many bidders should a publisher use? There is no fixed number. Add partners only when they provide incremental demand or strategic value without unacceptable latency or operational cost.

How does header bidding relate to an SSP? An SSP can participate as a demand pathway or help manage publisher inventory, auctions and marketplace controls depending on the platform architecture.

Programmatic Basics

Real-Time Bidding Explained: How Programmatic Ad Auctions Work

Understand real-time bidding, bid requests, auction decisioning, pricing, latency, privacy and how RTB fits within programmatic advertising.

Boost RAVA publishes educational content for advertisers and publishers. Examples explain strategy and technology; they are not performance guarantees.

RTB is an auction mechanism, not the whole of programmatic

Real-time bidding is one way programmatic advertising can transact digital inventory. When an eligible impression becomes available, information about the opportunity is sent through the ad-tech supply chain, buyers evaluate it and an auction can select a winning bid in a fraction of a second. Programmatic advertising is broader than RTB because it can also include private marketplaces, preferred deals and programmatic guaranteed arrangements.

Understanding that distinction matters for advertisers and publishers. RTB is useful when flexible auction-based decisioning is appropriate, but some campaigns need negotiated inventory, guaranteed delivery or tighter supply controls.

What happens in a bid request

A bid request can contain information about the placement, device, app or page context, supported creative sizes, auction rules and privacy or consent signals. Depending on the environment and applicable policy, additional permitted signals may be available to help a buyer decide whether the impression matches a campaign.

A responsible bidder should not treat every available field as equally useful. Context, placement quality, campaign eligibility, frequency controls and measurement strategy all influence whether an impression has value.

How a bidder makes a decision

The buying platform checks whether the opportunity is eligible for any active campaign. It can evaluate targeting rules, contextual relevance, budget, pacing, creative compatibility and estimated value. If the opportunity qualifies, the system submits a bid and creative reference according to the auction protocol.

Modern bidding systems may use machine learning to estimate conversion probability or expected value, but the model is constrained by campaign settings. The model should not override legal, privacy, brand-safety or budget controls.

Auction price and clearing logic

Different auction environments can use different pricing and deal rules. Advertisers should understand whether an auction is first-price, how floors are applied, which fees are visible and whether supply-path relationships affect the final cost. Publishers should understand how floors and deal priorities influence competition and fill.

A high bid is not automatically a good outcome if the impression is low quality. Both sides benefit from looking beyond CPM to metrics such as viewability, completion, conversion quality, invalid traffic and user experience.

Latency is part of auction quality

RTB decisions happen under strict time constraints. Slow integrations can miss auctions even when the underlying campaign would have been eligible. Infrastructure, geographic distance, endpoint performance and the number of supply-chain hops all affect latency.

For markets such as Bangladesh, where user connectivity can vary widely, end-to-end page and ad latency deserves special attention. Fast auction infrastructure should support the user experience rather than compete with it.

Privacy, consent and identity

RTB does not remove privacy obligations. Platforms need to respect consent signals, data-use restrictions and market-specific requirements. Contextual advertising can reduce dependence on identity-heavy targeting for some campaign goals, but it is not a universal substitute for every strategy.

Buyers and sellers should know what signals are passed through the auction, why they are needed and how long they are retained. Transparent data flows are increasingly important for commercial trust as well as compliance.

RTB across display, video, rich media and emerging screens

RTB can support standard display, online video and compatible rich-media opportunities. Connected TV and DOOH can also use programmatic auction concepts, although their inventory structures, creative requirements and measurement models differ from conventional web display.

Creative eligibility is therefore central to decisioning. An HTML5 interactive unit cannot be assumed to fit a CTV placement, and a DOOH creative must respect screen specifications and venue context. Programmatic infrastructure should understand those differences.

Frequently asked questions

Is RTB the same as programmatic advertising? No. RTB is one auction-based transaction method within the broader programmatic ecosystem.

How fast is an RTB auction? It typically operates in very short time windows, but exact timing varies by platform and supply path.

Can AI be used in RTB? Yes. Machine-learning models may assist with valuation, pacing and optimization, subject to campaign and policy controls.

Does the highest bidder always win? Auction rules, floors, deal priority, eligibility and platform logic can all affect the final decision.

CTV Advertising

Connected TV Advertising: A Programmatic CTV Growth Playbook

A practical CTV advertising guide covering programmatic buying, audience strategy, creative, measurement, frequency and Bangladesh-to-global campaign planning.

Boost RAVA publishes educational content for advertisers and publishers. Examples explain strategy and technology; they are not performance guarantees.

Why CTV belongs in a programmatic media plan

Connected TV brings internet-delivered television inventory into an environment where advertisers can apply programmatic planning and measurement. It combines the attention of television-style viewing with digital controls such as audience selection, pacing and reporting. That does not make CTV identical to web video; the screen, viewing context and inventory relationships are different.

For advertisers, the opportunity is to reach viewers on large screens while coordinating CTV with display, video, rich media or other channels. The challenge is to manage frequency and measurement so the campaign is genuinely incremental rather than simply duplicating exposure.

Inventory quality and supply path matter

CTV inventory can originate from apps, streaming services, device environments and programmatic marketplaces. Advertisers should understand what they are buying, whether the app or channel is identified, how the supply path is represented and what controls exist for unsuitable content or invalid traffic.

Private marketplace or curated supply arrangements can be useful when an advertiser needs more control. Open-auction access can add scale, but transparency should not be sacrificed for reach.

CTV creative should be designed for the television screen

A television viewing experience is usually lean-back and sound-enabled. Creative should communicate quickly, use readable text and respect the technical requirements of the placement. Repurposing a small mobile asset without adaptation can reduce clarity on a large screen.

Interactive behaviour also differs. Some CTV environments support limited interaction while others are primarily video experiences. Campaign teams should design the creative and call to action around what the actual device and app support.

Audience and contextual strategy

CTV targeting can use permitted audience signals, content context, geography, device information and deal-specific inventory criteria. Contextual signals can be particularly valuable when the surrounding programme or genre is relevant to the brand message.

Advertisers should avoid over-narrowing. Television-style reach can lose value if the campaign is constrained to tiny segments that cannot accumulate enough delivery or learning.

Measurement beyond completed views

Video completion rate is useful, but it is not a complete business outcome. CTV measurement may include reach, frequency, attention proxies, site visits, brand studies or conversion signals where technically and legally appropriate. The campaign objective should determine which metrics matter.

Cross-device attribution can be imperfect, so teams should document methodology and avoid presenting modelled outcomes as directly observed facts. Transparent measurement is more valuable than an impressive but unexplained number.

Frequency and cross-screen coordination

A viewer may encounter the same campaign on CTV, mobile web, apps and desktop. Without cross-screen planning, frequency can become excessive. Programmatic controls should aim to coordinate exposure where signals permit, while accepting that identity and device matching are not complete in every environment.

Creative sequencing can also help. CTV can introduce a brand story while display or rich media provides a later interactive step. The channels should have distinct roles instead of repeating the same asset everywhere.

CTV opportunities in Bangladesh and international campaigns

Bangladesh is a mobile-first digital market, but connected viewing continues to expand as streaming behaviour and smart-device adoption grow. Advertisers should plan CTV based on actual available inventory and audience behaviour rather than assuming television patterns from another country.

International campaigns need market-specific supply, language, regulation and measurement choices. A cross-market CTV plan should separate global brand consistency from local media execution.

Frequently asked questions

What is connected TV advertising? It is advertising delivered through internet-connected television environments such as smart TV apps and streaming devices.

Is CTV programmatic? CTV inventory can be bought programmatically, but not every CTV transaction uses an open auction.

Can CTV work with AI programmatic optimization? AI can assist with pacing, valuation, contextual classification and other decisions where data and platform capabilities support it.

Is CTV the same as online video? No. Both use video, but screen context, inventory, interaction and measurement differ.

Brand Safety

Brand Safety in Programmatic Advertising: Essential Practices

A practical guide to brand safety and suitability in programmatic advertising, including contextual controls, supply transparency, creative review and monitoring.

Boost RAVA publishes educational content for advertisers and publishers. Examples explain strategy and technology; they are not performance guarantees.

Brand safety and brand suitability are related but different

Brand safety focuses on avoiding environments that are broadly harmful or inappropriate for advertising. Brand suitability goes further by asking whether an otherwise acceptable environment fits a particular brand, campaign or audience. A news story can be legitimate and safe for many advertisers while still being unsuitable for a campaign with a sensitive message.

Programmatic teams should define both layers before launch. Generic blocklists alone are not enough because language and context change quickly, and overly broad blocking can exclude high-quality journalism or culturally relevant content.

Use contextual intelligence with human policy

Contextual classification can help understand page topics, sentiment and semantic meaning. AI can assist with that classification at scale, but policy decisions should remain explainable and reviewable. Campaign teams need documented categories, escalation rules and exceptions.

Contextual tools also need local awareness. A term may have different implications across markets or languages. Bangladesh-focused campaigns may require local-language review and regional knowledge that a generic global taxonomy misses.

Know the supply path

Supply-chain transparency helps advertisers understand how an impression reached the buying platform. Sellers.json, supply-chain objects and direct publisher relationships can provide useful signals. Fewer hops can improve transparency and sometimes latency, but quality should be judged from the full set of evidence rather than hop count alone.

Publishers also benefit from controlling which intermediaries are authorised to represent their inventory. Clean supply relationships make it easier for buyers to trust the marketplace.

Invalid traffic and domain or app spoofing

Brand safety is not only about content. Fraudulent or misrepresented inventory can waste budget and expose brands to environments they did not intend to buy. Buyers should use technical validation, inventory quality monitoring and trusted supply relationships to reduce the risk.

No system can promise that risk will be zero. A credible platform should describe controls and monitoring rather than guaranteeing perfect brand safety.

Creative safety matters too

Publishers need protection from malicious, misleading or technically disruptive creatives. Creative scanning, category controls and review workflows are part of a healthy marketplace. Advertisers should also verify that rich media and HTML5 units behave as intended across devices.

Interactive creative can add engagement, but it should not obscure disclosures, trap users or create unexpected redirects. User experience is part of brand quality.

Monitoring during the campaign

Pre-bid filters are important, but post-delivery monitoring is equally necessary. Review placements, apps, domains, categories, viewability and anomaly patterns. If a problem appears, campaign teams should be able to block, investigate and document the response quickly.

A useful review cadence depends on spend and risk. High-profile campaigns may need tighter monitoring than small always-on activity.

Balancing reach and protection

Overly restrictive controls can reduce scale and exclude legitimate content. Too little control can create unacceptable risk. The right balance depends on brand values, campaign objective, market and inventory type.

Instead of copying one universal blocklist, advertisers should define what matters to the specific campaign and update those rules as conditions change.

Frequently asked questions

Can AI guarantee brand safety? No. AI can help classify content and detect patterns, but governance, supply controls and human review remain important.

What is contextual brand suitability? It is the use of page or content meaning to judge whether an environment fits a specific brand or campaign.

Does brand safety apply to CTV and DOOH? Yes, although the relevant inventory signals and review methods differ from web display.

Should advertisers block all news? Usually not by default. A more nuanced suitability approach can protect the brand without unnecessarily excluding reputable news environments.

We should not describe every signage CMS as plug-and-play. Compatibility must be verified. If a native programmatic connector is unavailable, a Boost RAVA-compatible adapter or bridge must be configured before the screen is treated as programmatic inventory.

STEP-BY-STEP ADAPTER CONFIGURATION

Onboard the screen before you sell the slot

The exact menu names vary by signage CMS, but a production-ready DOOH integration generally needs the following sequence.

01

Link the adapter

Register the screen network or owner, generate the required integration credentials, then connect the compatible adapter/bridge to the signage CMS or player.

  • Network / account token
  • API credential where required
  • Device or player identity mapping
02

Describe the screen & venue

Programmatic demand needs reliable metadata to understand what the screen is and where it operates.

  • Screen ID and venue ID
  • Latitude / longitude
  • Venue type
  • Resolution, aspect ratio and orientation
  • Operating hours and supported media
03

Create the programmatic slot

Add an ad-source or programmatic placeholder to the approved playlist/loop rather than hard-coding a campaign file into the schedule.

  • Slot duration configured to the network
  • Creative type and resolution rules
  • Fallback content if no eligible ad returns
04

Cache, play and report

The player should download eligible media safely, play it at the scheduled slot and send supported playback callbacks or proof-of-play logs.

  • Local cache / prefetch
  • Timeout and retry rules
  • Playback event callback
  • Proof-of-play reconciliation
SCREEN & VENUE METADATA

Metadata is part of the inventory, not an optional note

IdentityScreen ID, player/device ID, network ID and venue ID where required.
LocationAccurate latitude/longitude, city/area and approved venue classification.
DisplayResolution, aspect ratio, orientation, screen type and supported image/video specifications.
Operating contextOperating hours, dayparts, audio capability, connection quality and venue restrictions.
Commercial controlsAvailability, approved pricing/floor rules, blocked categories and campaign eligibility.
MeasurementProof-of-play fields, supported audience measurement source and reporting identifiers.
Do not inflate audience numbers

A screen play is not automatically equal to a fixed number of people. Audience multipliers should only be used when a credible, approved measurement source supports them. Otherwise, report verified plays and the measurement that is actually available.

Configure for reliable playback, control and venue safety

SettingWhat to configureWhy it matters
Pricing / floorApproved minimum commercial rule for the screen or inventory package.Protects the inventory economics without inventing a universal CPM.

Category controlsVenue-appropriate blocklists and advertiser-category restrictions.Protects the screen environment and local compliance.
DaypartingAvailability windows such as commute, retail hours or event periods.Makes inventory reflect the real operating context.
FallbackHouse content or approved fallback when no eligible programmatic ad is returned.Keeps the signage loop healthy without blank screens.
Audience factorOnly use a multiplier when backed by an approved measurement source.Prevents unsupported impression inflation.

Do not call a screen live until the integration can prove playback

TEST

Sandbox / test creative
